name: Matthew
title: One of the Twelve
tagline: Called from the tax office: “Follow me.”
story: A tax collector whom Jesus called from his place at the receipt of custom; Mark and Luke call him Levi.

periods.title: With Jesus
periods.sub: The Gospels, in the harmony’s order

periods.title: After Scripture
periods.sub: Tradition, by who said it and when

entries.title: A tax office near Capernaum
entries.text: Mark tells the call straight after Jesus came back to Capernaum and went out “by the sea side”, so the tax office stood at or near Capernaum by the order of events. No verse names his home town.

entries.title: A publican
entries.text: A publican, a collector of taxes and tolls. He was “sitting at the receipt of custom” when Jesus called him, and Matthew's own list calls him “Matthew the publican”.

entries.title: Son of Alphaeus
entries.text: Mark names Levi's father: “Levi the son of Alphæus”.

entries.title: “The son” is supplied
entries.text: In the KJV the words “the son” are printed as a supplied word; the Greek gives only the father's name, literally Levi of Alphaeus.

The third tour of Galilee after instructing the Twelve and sending them forth by twos

entries.title: In the upper room
entries.text: He is named with the other apostles in the upper room in Jerusalem after the ascension.

entries.title: Never named again
entries.text: The last verse that names him is Acts 1:13. After that Acts speaks of “the eleven” and “the twelve” as a body (Acts 2:14; 6:2) but never names him again.

entries.title: Heracleon, quoted by Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 4.9
entries.text: Heracleon, a Valentinian teacher, argued that confessing Christ by one's life counts as well as confessing him aloud before the authorities, and named Matthew, Philip, Thomas and Levi in that argument. Schodde (ISBE, 1915) reads the passage as a plain denial that Matthew died a martyr.
entries.who: Heracleon, quoted by Clement of Alexandria, Stromata 4.9
entries.when: Heracleon about AD 170; Clement about AD 200

entries.title: Eusebius, Church History 3.24.6
entries.text: Eusebius writes that Matthew “had at first preached to the Hebrews”, and when he was about to go to other peoples wrote his Gospel in his native tongue.

entries.title: Socrates Scholasticus, Church History 1.19
entries.text: Socrates writes that when the apostles shared out the nations by lot, “Matthew was allotted Ethiopia”.

entries.title: Acts and Martyrdom of St. Matthew (Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 8)
entries.text: The Greek “Acts and Martyrdom of St. Matthew” tells of his preaching in the city of Myrna, where a king tries to burn him; the fire does not touch him and he dies in prayer. The translator calls it a much later work than the Acts of Andrew and Matthias, and notes that Matthew and Matthias are confused in these stories.
entries.who: Acts and Martyrdom of St. Matthew (Ante-Nicene Fathers, vol. 8)
entries.when: late; known from manuscripts of the 11th century and later

entries.title: The Contendings of the Apostles (Ethiopic), trans. Budge, pp. 130-136
entries.text: An Ethiopic “Martyrdom of Saint Matthew in Parthia” says he wrote a Gospel in Hebrew in Judaea, preached abroad, and was beheaded on a king's order.
entries.who: The Contendings of the Apostles (Ethiopic), trans. Budge, pp. 130-136
entries.when: Ethiopic version about the early 14th century; manuscript 15th century

accounts.title: The call at the tax office

verses.text: ¶ And as Jesus passed forth from thence, he saw a man, named Matthew, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he saith unto him, Follow me. And he arose, and followed him.
And as he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphæus sitting at the receipt of custom, and said unto him, Follow me. And he arose and followed him.
And he left all, rose up, and followed him.
¶ And as Jesus passed forth from thence, he saw a man, named Matthew, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he saith unto him, Follow me. And he arose, and followed him.
And as he passed by, he saw Levi the son of Alphæus sitting at the receipt of custom, and said unto him, Follow me. And he arose and followed him.
¶ And after these things he went forth, and saw a publican, named Levi, sitting at the receipt of custom: and he said unto him, Follow me.
And he left all, rose up, and followed him.

accounts.title: The feast with publicans and sinners

verses.text: ¶ And it came to pass, as Jesus sat at meat in the house, behold, many publicans and sinners came and sat down with him and his disciples.
And when the Pharisees saw it, they said unto his disciples, Why eateth your Master with publicans and sinners?
But when Jesus heard that, he said unto them, They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick.
But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.
And it came to pass, that, as Jesus sat at meat in his house, many publicans and sinners sat also together with Jesus and his disciples: for there were many, and they followed him.
And when the scribes and Pharisees saw him eat with publicans and sinners, they said unto his disciples, How is it that he eateth and drinketh with publicans and sinners?
When Jesus heard it, he saith unto them, They that are whole have no need of the physician, but they that are sick: I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.
And Levi made him a great feast in his own house: and there was a great company of publicans and of others that sat down with them.
But their scribes and Pharisees murmured against his disciples, saying, Why do ye eat and drink with publicans and sinners?
And Jesus answering said unto them, They that are whole need not a physician; but they that are sick.
I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.
Now the names of the twelve apostles are these; The first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother;
Philip, and Bartholomew; Thomas, and Matthew the publican; James the son of Alphaeus, and Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus;
Simon the Canaanite, and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him.
And Simon he surnamed Peter;
And James the son of Zebedee, and John the brother of James; and he surnamed them Boanerges, which is, The sons of thunder:
And Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus, and Simon the Canaanite,
And Judas Iscariot, which also betrayed him: and they went into an house.
Simon, (whom he also named Peter,) and Andrew his brother, James and John, Philip and Bartholomew,
Matthew and Thomas, James the son of Alphæus, and Simon called Zelotes,
And Judas the brother of James, and Judas Iscariot, which also was the traitor.

And when they were come in, they went up into an upper room, where abode both Peter, and James, and John, and Andrew, Philip, and Thomas, Bartholomew, and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon Zelotes, and Judas the brother of James.

items.q: Are Matthew and Levi the same man?
items.full: Are Matthew and Levi the same man? (Most widely held view first.)

views.label: One man
views.holders: Easton (1897); G. H. Schodde, ISBE (1915): “practically beyond all doubt”

argument.text: The three call stories agree in setting, words and sequence, and Mark's and Luke's lists of the Twelve include a Matthew but no Levi.

views.label: Two men
views.holders: Heracleon (about AD 170), as quoted by Clement of Alexandria (about AD 200)

argument.text: Heracleon names “Matthew, Philip, Thomas, Levi” as four separate examples.

items.q: Were Matthew and James son of Alphaeus brothers?
items.full: Were Matthew and James son of Alphaeus brothers? (In the order the sources give them.)

views.label: Brothers
views.holders: B. Weiss, as reported by A. W. Fortune (ISBE, 1915)

argument.text: Both are named as sons of an Alphaeus.

views.label: Not shown to be brothers
views.holders: G. H. Schodde and A. W. Fortune (ISBE, 1915)

argument.text: The lists call Peter and Andrew, and James and John, brothers, but never Matthew and James; the two may have had different fathers of the same name.

items.q: Did Matthew write the Gospel that bears his name?
items.full: Did Matthew write the Gospel that bears his name? (Earliest view first.)

views.label: Yes: he wrote it first in Hebrew, as the early church held
views.holders: Papias (died about AD 155), quoted by Eusebius; Irenaeus (about AD 180); Eusebius (about AD 325)

argument.text: Papias wrote that “Matthew wrote the oracles in the Hebrew language, and every one interpreted them as he was able”; Irenaeus that Matthew “issued a written Gospel among the Hebrews in their own dialect”.

views.label: Named after a Hebrew work of Matthew's that its writer used
views.holders: the theory Schodde (ISBE, 1915) calls “prevailing” in his day, though he disputes parts of it

argument.text: On this view Papias meant a collection, mainly of Jesus' sayings, that the writer of the Greek Gospel and Luke both used in Greek; the Gospel itself never names its author.

items.q: Is Matthew the Levi of Mark and Luke?
items.from: The identifications this page relies on

argument.text: This page treats Matthew and Levi as one man, as Easton (1897) and Schodde (ISBE, 1915) do: the three Gospels tell the same call, with the same words, at the same point in the story.

items.q: Matthew in one Gospel, Levi in two
items.from: The identifications this page relies on

argument.text: Only Matthew's Gospel calls the tax collector “Matthew”. Mark and Luke call him Levi when he is called, and Matthew in their lists of the Twelve, where no Levi appears.

items.q: Brother of James son of Alphaeus?
items.from: The identifications this page relies on

argument.text: The page does not make him the brother of James son of Alphaeus. Our person data links them, but no verse calls them brothers (see the question below).
